[www.yudkowsky.net](https://www.yudkowsky.net/)

**Eliezer Shlomo Yudkowsky** ( [_EL\-ee-EH\-zər yuud-KOW\-skee_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) born September 11, 1979) is an American [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") researcher[\[2\]](#cite_note-:0-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-:1-5) and writer on [decision theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_theory "Decision theory") and [ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics "Ethics"), known for popularizing ideas related to [friendly artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendly_artificial_intelligence "Friendly artificial intelligence").[\[6\]](#cite_note-aima-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-auto1-7) He is the founder of and a research fellow at the [Machine Intelligence Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_Intelligence_Research_Institute "Machine Intelligence Research Institute") (MIRI), a private research nonprofit based in [Berkeley, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California "Berkeley, California").[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

His work on the prospect of a runaway [intelligence explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_explosion "Intelligence explosion") influenced [philosopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosopher "Philosopher") [Nick Bostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Bostrom "Nick Bostrom")'s 2014 book _[Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence:_Paths,_Dangers,_Strategies "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies")_.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) His books include _[If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_Anyone_Builds_It,_Everyone_Dies:_Why_Superhuman_AI_Would_Kill_Us_All "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All")_, a [_New York Times_ bestseller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list") he co-authored with [Nate Soares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Soares "Nate Soares"),[\[10\]](#cite_note-hachette-10) as well as the _[Harry Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter "Harry Potter")_ fanfiction _[Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter_and_the_Methods_of_Rationality "Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality")_.

## Work in artificial intelligence safety

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Eliezer_Yudkowsky&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Work in artificial intelligence safety")\]

### Goal learning and incentives in software systems

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Eliezer_Yudkowsky&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Goal learning and incentives in software systems")\]

Yudkowsky's views on the safety challenges future generations of AI systems pose are discussed in [Stuart Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_J._Russell "Stuart J. Russell")'s and [Peter Norvig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Norvig "Peter Norvig")'s undergraduate textbook _[Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence:_A_Modern_Approach "Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach")_. Noting the difficulty of formally specifying general-purpose goals by hand, Russell and Norvig cite Yudkowsky's proposal that autonomous and adaptive systems be designed to learn correct behavior over time:

> Yudkowsky (2008)[\[11\]](#cite_note-gcr-11) goes into more detail about how to design a _Friendly AI_. He asserts that friendliness (a desire not to harm humans) should be designed in from the start, but that the designers should recognize both that their own designs may be flawed, and that the robot will learn and evolve over time. Thus the challenge is one of mechanism design—to design a mechanism for evolving AI under a system of checks and balances, and to give the systems utility functions that will remain friendly in the face of such changes.[\[6\]](#cite_note-aima-6)

In response to the [instrumental convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental_convergence "Instrumental convergence") concern, which implies that autonomous decision-making systems with poorly designed goals would have default incentives to mistreat humans, Yudkowsky and other MIRI researchers have recommended that work be done to specify software agents that converge on safe default behaviors even when their goals are misspecified.[\[12\]](#cite_note-corrigibility-12)[\[7\]](#cite_note-auto1-7) Yudkowsky also proposed in 2004 a theoretical [AI alignment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_alignment "AI alignment") framework called [coherent extrapolated volition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coherent_extrapolated_volition "Coherent extrapolated volition"), which involves designing AIs to pursue what people would desire under ideal [epistemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistemology "Epistemology") and moral conditions.[\[13\]](#cite_note-:2-13)

### Capabilities forecasting

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Eliezer_Yudkowsky&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Capabilities forecasting")\]

In the [intelligence explosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_explosion "Intelligence explosion") scenario hypothesized by [I. J. Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I._J._Good "I. J. Good"), recursively self-improving AI systems quickly transition from subhuman general intelligence to [superintelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence "Superintelligence"). [Nick Bostrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Bostrom "Nick Bostrom")'s 2014 book _[Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence:_Paths,_Dangers,_Strategies "Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies")_ sketches out Good's argument in detail, while citing Yudkowsky on the risk that [anthropomorphizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism "Anthropomorphism") advanced AI systems will cause people to misunderstand the nature of an intelligence explosion. "AI might make an _apparently_ sharp jump in intelligence purely as the result of anthropomorphism, the human tendency to think of 'village idiot' and 'Einstein' as the extreme ends of the intelligence scale, instead of nearly indistinguishable points on the scale of minds-in-general."[\[6\]](#cite_note-aima-6)[\[11\]](#cite_note-gcr-11)[\[13\]](#cite_note-:2-13)

In _Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach_, Russell and Norvig raise the objection that there are known limits to intelligent problem-solving from [computational complexity theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computational_complexity_theory "Computational complexity theory"); if there are strong limits on how efficiently algorithms can solve various tasks, an intelligence explosion may not be possible.[\[6\]](#cite_note-aima-6)

In a 2023 op-ed for [_Time_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_\(magazine\) "Time (magazine)"), Yudkowsky discussed the risks of artificial intelligence and advocated for international agreements to limit it, including an indefinite worldwide moratorium on large AI training runs.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) He suggested that participating countries should be willing to take military action, such as "destroy\[ing\] a rogue datacenter by airstrike", to enforce such a moratorium.[\[5\]](#cite_note-:1-5) The article helped introduce the debate about AI alignment to the mainstream, leading a reporter to ask President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") a question about AI safety at a press briefing.[\[2\]](#cite_note-:0-2)

### _If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies_

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Eliezer_Yudkowsky&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies")\]

Together with [Nate Soares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nate_Soares "Nate Soares"), Yudkowsky wrote _[If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_Anyone_Builds_It,_Everyone_Dies "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies")_, which was published by [Little, Brown and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little,_Brown_and_Company "Little, Brown and Company") on September 16, 2025.[\[10\]](#cite_note-hachette-10)

## Rationality writing

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Eliezer_Yudkowsky&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Rationality writing")\]

Between 2006 and 2009, Yudkowsky and [Robin Hanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Hanson "Robin Hanson") were the principal contributors to _Overcoming Bias_, a [cognitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cognitive "Cognitive") and [social science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science") blog sponsored by the [Future of Humanity Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_of_Humanity_Institute "Future of Humanity Institute") of [Oxford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University"). In February 2009, Yudkowsky founded _[LessWrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LessWrong "LessWrong")_, a "community blog devoted to refining the art of human [rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality "Rationality")".[\[16\]](#cite_note-miller-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-businessinsider-17) _Overcoming Bias_ has since functioned as Hanson's personal blog, while _LessWrong_ has grown into the main online hub for the [rationalist community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalist_community "Rationalist community").

Over 300 blog posts by Yudkowsky on philosophy and science (originally written on _LessWrong_ and _Overcoming Bias_) were released as an ebook, _Rationality: From AI to Zombies_, by MIRI in 2015.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) This book is also referred to as "The Sequences".[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) MIRI has also published _Inadequate Equilibria_, Yudkowsky's 2017 ebook on societal inefficiencies.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

Yudkowsky has also written several works of fiction. His [fanfiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fan_fiction "Fan fiction") novel _[Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter_and_the_Methods_of_Rationality "Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality")_ uses plot elements from [J. K. Rowling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._K._Rowling "J. K. Rowling")'s _[Harry Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter "Harry Potter")_ series to illustrate topics in science and rationality.[\[16\]](#cite_note-miller-16)[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

Yudkowsky is an [autodidact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodidacticism "Autodidacticism").[\[23\]](#cite_note-vox-23) He dropped out of middle school due to chronic health issues,[\[24\]](#cite_note-24) and did not attend high school or college.[\[25\]](#cite_note-25) He is Jewish and was raised [Modern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Orthodox_Judaism "Modern Orthodox Judaism"), but is now [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular "Secular").[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)

### https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_mass
# Solar mass

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Solar mass

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Sun_vs_planets.svg/250px-Sun_vs_planets.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sun_vs_planets.svg)

The Sun contains 99.86% of the mass of the Solar System. Bodies less massive than [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn") are not visible at this scale. [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")'s mass (0.10%) is actually more than three times Saturn's (0.03%), which cannot accurately be seen in this graphic.

General information

[Unit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_units_of_measurement "System of units of measurement")

[Astronomical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_system_of_units "Astronomical system of units")

Unit of

[mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass")

Symbol

M☉

In [SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit")

1.988416×1030 kg[\[1\]](#cite_note-Quantities-1)

The **solar mass** (**M☉**) is a frequently used [unit of mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass#Units_of_mass "Mass") in [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy"), equal to approximately 2×1030 [kg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram"). It is approximately equal to the mass of the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"). It is often used to indicate the masses of other [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star"), as well as [stellar clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_cluster "Star cluster"), [nebulae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebula "Nebula"), [galaxies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy "Galaxy") and [black holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole "Black hole"). More precisely, the mass of the Sun is as follows:

nominal solar mass M☉ = 1.988416×1030 kg or a best estimate of M☉ = (1.988475±0.000092)×1030 kg.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Quantities-1)

The solar mass is about 333000 times the [mass of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass") (M🜨), or 1047 times the [mass of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_mass "Jupiter mass") (MJ).

## History of measurement

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Solar_mass&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of measurement")\]

The value of the gravitational constant was first derived from measurements that were made by [Henry Cavendish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cavendish "Henry Cavendish") in 1798 with a [torsion balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion_balance "Torsion balance").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) The value he obtained differs by only 1% from the modern value, but was not as precise.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) The [diurnal parallax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallax#Diurnal_parallax "Parallax") of the Sun was accurately measured during the transits of Venus in 1761 and 1769,[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) yielding a value of 9″ (9 [arcseconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_and_second_of_arc "Minute and second of arc"), compared to the present value of 8.794148″). From the value of the diurnal parallax, one can determine the distance to the Sun from the geometry of Earth.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

The first known estimate of the solar mass was by [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) In his work _[Principia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica")_ (1687), he estimated that the ratio of the mass of Earth to the Sun was about 1:28700. Later he determined that his value was based upon a faulty value for the solar parallax, which he had used to estimate the distance to the Sun. He corrected his estimated ratio to 1:169282 in the third edition of the _Principia_. The current value for the solar parallax is smaller still, yielding an estimated mass ratio of 1:332946.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

As a unit of measurement, the solar mass came into use before the astronomical unit and the gravitational constant were precisely measured. This is because the relative mass of another planet in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") or the combined mass of two [binary stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_star#Use_in_astrophysics "Binary star") can be calculated in units of Solar mass directly from the orbital radius and orbital period of the planet or stars using Kepler's third law.

The mass of the Sun cannot be measured directly and is instead calculated from other measurable factors, using the equation for the [orbital period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_period "Orbital period") of a small body orbiting a central mass.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Based on the length of the year, the distance from Earth to the Sun (an [astronomical unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") or au), and the [gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant "Gravitational constant") (_G_), the mass of the Sun is given by solving [Kepler's third law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler's_laws_of_planetary_motion "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"):[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) ![{\\displaystyle M\_{\\odot }={\\frac {4\\pi ^{2}\\times (1~{\\text{au}})^{3}}{G\\times (1~{\\text{yr}})^{2}}}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4c4d24461b50db7c503ee8fbb6c41841594606a6)

The value of _G_ is difficult to measure and is only known with limited accuracy (_see_ [Cavendish experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavendish_experiment "Cavendish experiment")). The value of _G_ times the mass of an object, called the [standard gravitational parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gravitational_parameter "Standard gravitational parameter"), is known for the Sun and several planets to a much higher accuracy than _G_ alone.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) As a result, the solar mass is used as the standard mass in the [astronomical system of units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_system_of_units "Astronomical system of units").

The Sun is losing mass because of [fusion reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") occurring within its core, leading to the emission of [electromagnetic energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiant_energy "Radiant energy") and neutrinos, and by the ejection of matter with the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind"). It is expelling about (2–3)×10−14 M☉/year.[\[14\]](#cite_note-carroll_ostlie1995-14) The mass loss rate will increase when the Sun enters the [red giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_giant "Red giant") stage, climbing to (7–9)×10−14 M☉/year when it reaches the [tip of the red-giant branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tip_of_the_red-giant_branch "Tip of the red-giant branch"). This will rise to 10−6 M☉/year on the [asymptotic giant branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_giant_branch "Asymptotic giant branch"), before peaking at a rate of 10−5 to 10−4 M☉/year as the Sun generates a [planetary nebula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nebula "Planetary nebula"). By the time the Sun becomes a degenerate [white dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_dwarf "White dwarf"), it will have lost 46% of its starting mass.[\[15\]](#cite_note-mnras361-15)

The mass of the Sun has been decreasing since the time it formed. This occurs through two processes in nearly equal amounts. First, in the [Sun's core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_core "Solar core"), hydrogen is converted into helium through [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion"), in particular the [p–p chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton–proton_chain "Proton–proton chain"), and this reaction converts some mass into energy in the form of [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray") photons. Most of this energy eventually [radiates away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_luminosity "Solar luminosity") from the Sun. Second, high-energy protons and electrons in the atmosphere of the Sun are ejected directly into outer space as the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind") and [coronal mass ejections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronal_mass_ejection "Coronal mass ejection").[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

The original mass of the Sun at the time it reached the [main sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence "Main sequence") remains uncertain.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) The early Sun had much higher mass-loss rates than at present, and it may have lost anywhere from 1–7% of its natal mass over the course of its main-sequence lifetime.[\[18\]](#cite_note-apj583_2_1024-18)

One solar mass, M☉, can be converted to related units:[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

*   27068510 M☾ ([Lunar mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_mass "Lunar mass"))
*   332946 M🜨 ([Earth mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass"))
*   1047.35 MJ ([Jupiter mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_mass "Jupiter mass"))

It is also frequently useful in [general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity") to express mass in units of length or time.

*   M☉_G_/_c_2 ≈ 1.48 km (half the [Schwarzschild radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_radius "Schwarzschild radius") of the Sun)

cascade.findings: Claim is well-supported by labor history sources and is not misleading. The AFL was founded in 1886 as a loose federation of craft unions under Samuel Gompers, dedicated to principles of craft unionism https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Its approximately 100 national and international unions retained full autonomy and each received "exclusive jurisdiction" over a craft, with "one union per craft; one craft per union," which produced bitter jurisdictional disputes between affiliates https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Craft unions are described as organizing by specific craft/trade (e.g., all carpenters in carpenters' union, plasterers in plasterers' union) with own administration, agreements and halls https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Coming out of guild tradition, they policed how work was done by "maintaining standards for admission into the trade; requiring entrants to go through an apprenticeship program controlled by the union, rather than the employer; and dictating the processes, tools, standards, and pace of work" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Related summaries note membership was exclusive to those with particular skills to maintain strong control over labor supply in specialized areas, limiting membership to skilled workers and excluding unskilled workers, with craft exclusivity creating barriers to entry https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . AFL unions required union members only via closed shop and "Selective admission to apprenticeships restricted membership, thereby artificially limiting the supply of skilled labor" is the standard textbook description of early trade-union control.

Condoms were low-value consumer goods sold in pharmacies, described as a scarce commodity where some people bought for future use and others resold at higher price https://nevsedoma.com.ua/ , and chronic shortage of condoms (called "Article Number 2") https://photius.com/ . Practical constraint was supply/availability ("whatever I could get"), not a legal quota. cascade.findings: Claim is directionally true as a first-order expectation (if per-ask acceptance probability p is constant, expected dates = n*p), but "approximately linear" overstates precision and ignores documented non-linearities. Average match-to-date conversion is only 10-15%, with 60-70% of matches never exchanging messages and users needing 50-100 matches to secure one actual date https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics - more attempts do yield more dates on average, supporting monotonicity. However: 1) Selectivity improves outcomes - being slightly pickier (30-50% swipe-right rate) leads to better match quality and conversation rates than swiping right on everyone, contradicting simple "lower standards = proportionally more dates" https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . 2) More matches don't necessarily mean more success - women receive 5-10x more matches than men but converting attention into quality dates is just as challenging https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . 3) Rejection mind-set experiments show acceptance chance falls on average 27% from first to last partner option, explained by decline in satisfaction with pictures and perceived dating success, with people gradually "closing off" from opportunities https://www.researchgate.net/publication/335312368_A_Rejection_Mind-Set_Choice_Overload_in_Online_Dating . 4) Logic of diminishing returns: being presented with the 250th option does not add as much benefit as the 12th, leading to decreased satisfaction, increased regret, decision complexity and cognitive load https://abcwest.sitehost.iu.edu/pmwiki/pdf/lenton.shoppingcart.2010.pdf . Average ROI is also poor (90 minutes daily for ~one date per month) with burnout/paradox of choice https://checklovers.com/blog/dating-statistics/online-dating-success-rate-statistics . So linearity is a rough heuristic, not an empirical scaling law; returns diminish with volume/effort.

## Research findings

Rovell's tweet compares two different and incompatible statistics. For the 2026 Finals, multiple outlets confirm Game 5 of the Knicks-Spurs series averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million late in the telecast as the Knicks rallied to win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years). 33 million is a simultaneous, average-minute peak audience figure. Dividing by the current U.S. population (~346M) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching Rovell's number.

For the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6, Wikipedia's list of NBA Finals ratings states the game averaged a 22.3 rating/38 share and 35.89 million viewers, making it the highest-rated and most-watched NBA game on record (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings). However, the 1998 NBA playoffs Wikipedia page separately notes it was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA history, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). Contemporary reporting from the Washington Post confirms NBC estimated that 72 million people watched all or part of the game, a figure based on cumulative reach across the whole broadcast, not a simultaneous peak (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). 72 million divided by the roughly 276 million U.S. population in 1998 comes out to about 26.1%, matching Rovell's cited figure precisely — meaning he used the 'watched any portion' cumulative reach number for 1998, not a comparable simultaneous peak.

This is an apples-to-oranges comparison: Rovell pairs the 2026 game's simultaneous peak-minute audience (33M) against the 1998 game's cumulative total reach across the whole broadcast (72M watched at least part of the game). Cumulative reach is always substantially larger than any single-minute peak, so using it for 1998 while using true peak for 2026 inflates the apparent gap between the two eras. If both were calculated the same way — e.g., comparing average viewership, where 1998 drew 35.89 million (about 13% of the 1998 population) against 2026's average of 24.5 million for Game 5 or 20.6 million for the series (about 6-7% of today's population) — the disparity implied would look notably different from the 26.1% vs 9.5% framing in the tweet, though 1998 would still be clearly higher either way. Separately, all sources agree the 2026 Knicks-Spurs series was the most-watched NBA Finals since 1998, averaging 20.6 million viewers across the five games (https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years), so the broader point that 1998 drew a proportionally far larger audience is directionally correct, but the specific percentages Rovell cites conflate incompatible metrics (peak audience vs. cumulative total reach), which could mislead readers about the actual scale of the viewership gap.

# Knicks NBA Championship Game Draws 24.5 Million Viewers

Knicks in 5…and nearly 25 million viewers.

According to Nielsen data, the [New York Knicks](https://variety.com/t/new-york-knicks/) victory in game five of the 2026 NBA Finals over the San Antonio Spurs drew 24.5 million viewers across [ABC](https://variety.com/t/abc/) and [ESPN](https://variety.com/t/espn/). The game, which aired on June 13, peaked at 33 million viewers late in the telecast as the Knicks staged a rally to come back for a 94-90 victory.

That is the most-watched NBA Finals game five since 1998, when Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls defeated the Utah Jazz. That series ultimately went to game six, with the Bulls coming out on top.

The Knicks-Spurs finals averaged approximately 20.6 million viewers across all five games. That is double the roughly 10.3 million average for the 2025 finals, in which the Oklahoma City Thunder defeated the Indiana Pacers. The final three games of this year’s finals all drew more than 20 million viewers as well.

The Knicks won their first NBA Championship since 1973 on Saturday night, with Knicks guard Jalen Brunson carrying the team with 45 points scored. Brunson was named Finals MVP for his efforts.

Although the game took place in San Antonio, Knicks fans were out in force at the game. Celebrities like Ben Stiller, Sydney Sweeney, Timothée Chalamet, and Spike Lee were all in attendance to see the team clinch the victory.

Back in New York, New Yorkers were jubilant to say the least following the victory, with thousands taking to the streets til the wee hours of the morning to celebrate the win.

The **1998 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association")'s [1997–98 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_NBA_season "1997–98 NBA season"). The tournament concluded with the two-time defending NBA champion and [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_\(NBA\) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") champion [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") defeating the [Western Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Conference_\(NBA\) "Western Conference (NBA)") champion [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") 4 games to 2 in the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals"). The Bulls achieved a second three peat, a goal unrivaled since the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") in [1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NBA_playoffs "1966 NBA playoffs"). Michael Jordan was named [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player_Award "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award") for the sixth and final time.

The [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") made the playoffs for the first time since [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993–94_New_Jersey_Nets_season "1993–94 New Jersey Nets season"), but did not appear again until [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NBA_playoffs "2002 NBA playoffs"). Their presence was a mere asterisk compared to what they accomplished in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001–02_New_Jersey_Nets_season "2001–02 New Jersey Nets season"), getting swept by the eventual champion Bulls.

The Minnesota Timberwolves won their first playoff game in franchise history by winning Game 2 of their series against the Seattle SuperSonics. However, the SuperSonics prevailed in five games despite the Timberwolves taking a 2–1 series lead.

The [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") lost to Indiana in the first round 3–1 and did not appear again until [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005–06_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2005–06 Cleveland Cavaliers season"). It would also be the final playoff appearance for the Cavaliers without [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James "LeBron James") on the roster.

The Heat–Knicks series was extremely notable for two reasons

*   Game 4: A fight broke out between [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_\(basketball,_born_1969\) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)") and [Alonzo Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Mourning "Alonzo Mourning") at the end of the game (in which the Knicks won 90–85). A lasting image of the fight was Knicks coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") clinging to Mourning's leg. Both players were suspended for two games. Johnson and Mourning had bad blood dating back to their stint as [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") teammates.
*   Game 5: The New York Knicks became the fourth seventh seed to knock off a second seeded team in the first round of the playoffs. This would not occur again until [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_playoffs "2010 NBA playoffs").

Game 5 of the Jazz–Rockets series would be the final game of [Clyde Drexler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler")'s career.

The [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1997–98 Los Angeles Lakers season") advanced to the Western Conference Finals for the first time since [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990–91_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1990–91 Los Angeles Lakers season"). They were ultimately swept by the Jazz.

The [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Indiana_Pacers_season "1997–98 Indiana Pacers season") entered the postseason with a franchise record 58 wins. Although they would lose to the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") in the Eastern Conference Finals, this team was later named by Pacers.com as the greatest in franchise history primarily due to their record, even better than the [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999–2000_Indiana_Pacers_season "1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season") team that won the Eastern Conference Title. The Eastern Conference Finals series between the Chicago Bulls and Indiana Pacers was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   Game 4: [Reggie Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Miller "Reggie Miller")'s game winning 3 pointer with 0.7 seconds, which has been marked one of the greatest postseason moments in NBA History. Michael Jordan attempted a game winning 3 pointer of his own, but it rimmed out, effectively tying the series at 2–2.
*   Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals: With a win, the Pacers took the Bulls to the limit by becoming 1 of only 2 teams to force a Game 7 in the Bulls' title years (the [Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991–92_New_York_Knicks_season "1991–92 New York Knicks season") achieved this in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_NBA_playoffs "1992 NBA playoffs")).
*   Game 7: This was the first (and as of 2025, only) Game 7 to take place at the [United Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Center "United Center").[](https://www.nba.com/pacers/running-at-the-bulls-oral-history-1997-98-pacers-pt-2)
*   Game 7: This was the last Game 7 the Bulls would play until [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_playoffs "2009 NBA playoffs").

For the first time since [1989 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NBA_Finals "1989 NBA Finals"), there was a rematch of the same two teams: the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") and the [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"). This would not happen again until [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_Finals "2014 NBA Finals").

[Game 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_6_of_the_1998_NBA_Finals "Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals") of the NBA Finals was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   In the waning moments of the game [Michael Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") made the title winning shot over [Bryon Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryon_Russell "Bryon Russell"). This moment was marked as one of the greatest moments in NBA playoff history.
*   It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S.
*   It was the last Chicago Bulls postseason game until [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_playoffs "2005 NBA playoffs") and the last involving the Michael Jordan-led Bulls.
*   Michael Jordan's final NBA playoff game.
*   [Phil Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Jackson "Phil Jackson")'s final game as coach of the Chicago Bulls (he would go on to coach the Los Angeles Lakers two seasons later).
*   As of 2026, this remains the most recent NBA Finals game for the Chicago Bulls and the Utah Jazz.

## Post

At its height, 9.5 percent of the U.S. population was watching Knicks-Spurs. 

To put in perspective, 26.1 percent of the U.S. population was watching Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Rovell's tweet compares two different and incompatible statistics. For the 2026 Finals, multiple outlets confirm Game 5 of the Knicks-Spurs series averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million late in the telecast as the Knicks rallied to win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years). 33 million is a simultaneous, average-minute peak audience figure. Dividing by the current U.S. population (~346M) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching Rovell's number.

For the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6, Wikipedia's list of NBA Finals ratings states the game averaged a 22.3 rating/38 share and 35.89 million viewers, making it the highest-rated and most-watched NBA game on record (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings). However, the 1998 NBA playoffs Wikipedia page separately notes it was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA history, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). cascade.findings: Post claims peak audience was 9.5% of US population for Knicks-Spurs (2026) and 26.1% for Bulls-Jazz (1998). First part is roughly accurate: ESPN reported Knicks 94-90 Game 5 win averaged 24.5 million and peaked at 33 million https://www.espn.ph/nba/story/_/id/49086824/knicks-title-clinching-win-vs-spurs-most-watched-nba-finals-game-5-1998 and that the series averaged 20.6 million, highest since 1998 when Bulls-Jazz averaged 29.04 million https://www.espn.ph/nba/story/_/id/49086824/knicks-title-clinching-win-vs-spurs-most-watched-nba-finals-game-5-1998 . US population forecast for Dec 2026 is 342.594 million https://www.ceicdata.com/en/indicator/united-states/forecast-population . 33 / 342.594 = ~9.6%, so 9.5% is reasonable rounding. Second part is false by ~2x: Bulls-Jazz Game 6 in 1998 averaged 35.9 million viewers, the all-time NBA high https://www.sportsbusinessjournal.com/Journal/Issues/2016/06/27/Media/NBA-audiences.aspx . US had 270.4 million residents on July 1, 1998 https://migration.ucdavis.edu/mn/more.php?id=1696 . 35.9 / 270.4 = ~13.3% (using 274.5m alternate estimate still ~13.1%), not 26.1%. 26.1% of ~270-275m would require ~70-72 million viewers, nearly double the actual record. Author likely confused Nielsen household rating (Game 6 did 22.3 rating) with share of population. Comparison therefore exaggerates 1998 relative dominance (~2.75x vs actual ~1.4x).

# BULLS A WINNER FOR NBC

FINAL IS TOP-RATED PRO HOOP GAME EVER

June 16, 1998 More than**28 years ago**

By David Bauder

NEW YORK, JUNE 16 -- The Chicago Bulls victory that clinched the NBA championship was the highest-rated pro basketball game ever broadcast.

Sunday's sixth and final game in the series with the Utah Jazz had a 22.3 rating and 38 percent audience share, with NBC estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it. The previous top-rated NBA broadcast was the seventh game of the Finals between the Detroit Pistons and Los Angeles Lakers in 1988.

The Bulls-Jazz series was the highest-rated NBA Finals series ever, topping the Bulls-Phoenix Suns series of 1993, NBC said.

About the only bad news for NBC was that Michael Jordan's final shot eliminated the need for a highly rated seventh game.

NBC easily won Nielsen Media Research's prime-time ratings race last week. The top 12 shows were all on NBC, although this was padded with the inclusion of three NBA pregame shows and one post-game show. Nielsen counts these in the ratings separately from the games.

For the week, NBC had an 11.7 rating and 21 share. CBS was a distant second at 6.9/12, ABC had a 6.0/11, Fox a 4.4/8, WB a 2.4/4 and UPN a 2.1/4.

CBS's "48 Hours" newsmagazine, which reported on the investigation into Princess Diana's death, tied for its highest rating of the year, and finished just under a competing rerun of "ER."

Fox's plans to include more original programming this summer can't come soon enough for the network. Some of its biggest series, like "The X-Files" and "King of the Hill," have seen their audiences sliced in half with reruns. The **1998 NBA playoffs** was the postseason tournament of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association")'s [1997–98 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_NBA_season "1997–98 NBA season"). The tournament concluded with the two-time defending NBA champion and [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_\(NBA\) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") champion [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bulls "Chicago Bulls") defeating the [Western Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Conference_\(NBA\) "Western Conference (NBA)") champion [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Jazz "Utah Jazz") 4 games to 2 in the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals"). The Bulls achieved a second three peat, a goal unrivaled since the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") in [1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_NBA_playoffs "1966 NBA playoffs"). Michael Jordan was named [NBA Finals MVP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_Most_Valuable_Player_Award "NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Award") for the sixth and final time.

The [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Nets "Brooklyn Nets") made the playoffs for the first time since [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993–94_New_Jersey_Nets_season "1993–94 New Jersey Nets season"), but did not appear again until [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_NBA_playoffs "2002 NBA playoffs"). Their presence was a mere asterisk compared to what they accomplished in [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001–02_New_Jersey_Nets_season "2001–02 New Jersey Nets season"), getting swept by the eventual champion Bulls.

The Minnesota Timberwolves won their first playoff game in franchise history by winning Game 2 of their series against the Seattle SuperSonics. However, the SuperSonics prevailed in five games despite the Timberwolves taking a 2–1 series lead.

The [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") lost to Indiana in the first round 3–1 and did not appear again until [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005–06_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2005–06 Cleveland Cavaliers season"). It would also be the final playoff appearance for the Cavaliers without [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James "LeBron James") on the roster.

The Heat–Knicks series was extremely notable for two reasons

*   Game 4: A fight broke out between [Larry Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Johnson_\(basketball,_born_1969\) "Larry Johnson (basketball, born 1969)") and [Alonzo Mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alonzo_Mourning "Alonzo Mourning") at the end of the game (in which the Knicks won 90–85). A lasting image of the fight was Knicks coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") clinging to Mourning's leg. Both players were suspended for two games. Johnson and Mourning had bad blood dating back to their stint as [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") teammates.
*   Game 5: The New York Knicks became the fourth seventh seed to knock off a second seeded team in the first round of the playoffs. This would not occur again until [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_playoffs "2010 NBA playoffs").

Game 5 of the Jazz–Rockets series would be the final game of [Clyde Drexler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler")'s career.

The [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1997–98 Los Angeles Lakers season") advanced to the Western Conference Finals for the first time since [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990–91_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1990–91 Los Angeles Lakers season"). They were ultimately swept by the Jazz.

The [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Indiana_Pacers_season "1997–98 Indiana Pacers season") entered the postseason with a franchise record 58 wins. Although they would lose to the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") in the Eastern Conference Finals, this team was later named by Pacers.com as the greatest in franchise history primarily due to their record, even better than the [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999–2000_Indiana_Pacers_season "1999–2000 Indiana Pacers season") team that won the Eastern Conference Title. The Eastern Conference Finals series between the Chicago Bulls and Indiana Pacers was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   Game 4: [Reggie Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Miller "Reggie Miller")'s game winning 3 pointer with 0.7 seconds, which has been marked one of the greatest postseason moments in NBA History. Michael Jordan attempted a game winning 3 pointer of his own, but it rimmed out, effectively tying the series at 2–2.
*   Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals: With a win, the Pacers took the Bulls to the limit by becoming 1 of only 2 teams to force a Game 7 in the Bulls' title years (the [Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991–92_New_York_Knicks_season "1991–92 New York Knicks season") achieved this in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_NBA_playoffs "1992 NBA playoffs")).
*   Game 7: This was the first (and as of 2025, only) Game 7 to take place at the [United Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Center "United Center").[](https://www.nba.com/pacers/running-at-the-bulls-oral-history-1997-98-pacers-pt-2)
*   Game 7: This was the last Game 7 the Bulls would play until [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_playoffs "2009 NBA playoffs").

For the first time since [1989 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_NBA_Finals "1989 NBA Finals"), there was a rematch of the same two teams: the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997–98 Chicago Bulls season") and the [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"). This would not happen again until [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_Finals "2014 NBA Finals").

[Game 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_6_of_the_1998_NBA_Finals "Game 6 of the 1998 NBA Finals") of the NBA Finals was extremely notable for several reasons:

*   In the waning moments of the game [Michael Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jordan "Michael Jordan") made the title winning shot over [Bryon Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryon_Russell "Bryon Russell"). This moment was marked as one of the greatest moments in NBA playoff history.
*   It was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S.
*   It was the last Chicago Bulls postseason game until [2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_playoffs "2005 NBA playoffs") and the last involving the Michael Jordan-led Bulls.
*   Michael Jordan's final NBA playoff game.
*   [Phil Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Jackson "Phil Jackson")'s final game as coach of the Chicago Bulls (he would go on to coach the Los Angeles Lakers two seasons later).
*   As of 2026, this remains the most recent NBA Finals game for the Chicago Bulls and the Utah Jazz.

# Knicks-Spurs delivers most-watched NBA Finals since 1998

### 2026 NBA Finals

The 2026 NBA Finals averaged more than 20 million viewers on ABC/ESPN to cap off the most-watched NBA postseason since 1998.

Official release

June 16, 2026 9:27 PM

The Knicks defeat the Spurs in Game 5 to win the Finals and claim their first NBA championship in 53 years.

**NEW YORK** – The 2026 NBA Finals between the New York Knicks and San Antonio Spurs was the most-watched NBA Finals in 28 years (since 1998), averaging 20.6 million viewers on ABC and ESPN. The series generated multi-decade highs and records across television viewership, social media engagement and merchandise sales. Highlights include:

### Viewership

*   Game 5, which saw the Knicks capture their first NBA championship in 53 years, **averaged 24.5 million viewers** and **peaked at 33 million viewers at 11:15 p.m. ET**, marking the most-watched NBA Finals Game 5 since 1998.
*   In addition to the most-watched NBA Finals since 1998, the league also saw its most-watched postseason in 28 years across ABC/ESPN, Amazon Prime Video and NBC/Peacock.
*   The NBA Finals on ABC and ESPN delivered the highest share for a Finals on record (38.3).

![](https://cdn.nba.com/manage/2026/06/HK9rghjWMAE4TMW-441x588.jpeg)

### Social / Digital

*   The five-game series generated a **record 15 billion views** and counting on social media, the most ever for an NBA Finals and nearly triple the previous record set in 2025.
*   Game 5 generated more than **4 billion views**, surpassing the previous single-game record set during Game 4.
*   The 2026 NBA Finals continued a record-setting postseason on social media, highlighted by a record eight postseason games surpassing **one billion views**.

![](https://cdn.nba.com/manage/2026/06/HK9wnilWMAEo1P0-441x588.jpeg)

### Merchandise

*   In the first 24 hours following their clinching win in Game 5, the Knicks set an **all-time Fanatics merchandise record** for any championship team ever across all sports.
*   The 2026 NBA Finals set a new league record for merchandise sales across NBAStore.com, Fanatics, team stores and third-party retail. Finals merchandise sales doubled the previous NBA Finals record set in 2020.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Rovell's tweet compares two different and incompatible statistics. For the 2026 Finals, multiple outlets confirm Game 5 of the Knicks-Spurs series averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million late in the telecast as the Knicks rallied to win (https://variety.com/2026/tv/ratings/knicks-nba-championship-game-ratings-1236783260/, https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years). 33 million is a simultaneous, average-minute peak audience figure. Dividing by the current U.S. population (~346M) yields almost exactly 9.5%, matching Rovell's number.

For the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6, Wikipedia's list of NBA Finals ratings states the game averaged a 22.3 rating/38 share and 35.89 million viewers, making it the highest-rated and most-watched NBA game on record (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings). However, the 1998 NBA playoffs Wikipedia page separately notes it was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA history, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). Contemporary reporting from the Washington Post confirms NBC estimated that 72 million people watched all or part of the game, a figure based on cumulative reach across the whole broadcast, not a simultaneous peak (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). 72 million divided by the roughly 276 million U.S. population in 1998 comes out to about 26.1%, matching Rovell's cited figure precisely — meaning he used the 'watched any portion' cumulative reach number for 1998, not a comparable simultaneous peak.

This is an apples-to-oranges comparison: Rovell pairs the 2026 game's simultaneous peak-minute audience (33M) against the 1998 game's cumulative total reach across the whole broadcast (72M watched at least part of the game). Cumulative reach is always substantially larger than any single-minute peak, so using it for 1998 while using true peak for 2026 inflates the apparent gap between the two eras. If both were calculated the same way — e.g., comparing average viewership, where 1998 drew 35.89 million (about 13% of the 1998 population) against 2026's average of 24.5 million for Game 5 or 20.6 million for the series (about 6-7% of today's population) — the disparity implied would look notably different from the 26.1% vs 9.5% framing in the tweet, though 1998 would still be clearly higher either way. Separately, all sources agree the 2026 Knicks-Spurs series was the most-watched NBA Finals since 1998, averaging 20.6 million viewers across the five games (https://www.nba.com/news/nba-finals-2026-viewership-most-watched-28-years), so the broader point that 1998 drew a proportionally far larger audience is directionally correct, but the specific percentages Rovell cites conflate incompatible metrics (peak audience vs. cumulative total reach), which could mislead readers about the actual scale of the viewership gap.

## Penny Hofstadter

  
**Penelope "Penny" Hofstadter** is the show _The Big Bang Theory_'s first and always main female protagonist. She lives in [Apartment 4B](/wiki/Apartment_4B "Apartment 4B") with her husband Leonard Hofstadter across the hall from Sheldon Cooper, who lives in apartment 4A where Leonard used to live with Sheldon as roommates. Although the sleeping arrangements are a little complicated. This was an accommodation for Sheldon who was having a very hard time dealing with his break-up with Amy, and Leonard moving out in The 2003 Approximation. Leonard also maintains an office in 4A. Her full first name is possibly "Penelope" as implied by "[The Barbarian Sublimation](/wiki/The_Barbarian_Sublimation "The Barbarian Sublimation")", and her maiden name has never been revealed. But due to her recent marriage to Leonard, her last name is Hofstadter. For a while her last name was Johnson while unknowingly married to ex-boyfriend Zack Johnson. That marriage was annulled in [The Thanksgiving Decoupling](/wiki/The_Thanksgiving_Decoupling "The Thanksgiving Decoupling").

An aspiring, but mostly unsuccessful actress, she was born on a farm near Omaha, Nebraska, and worked at The Cheesecake Factory as a waitress until she quit in "[The Occupation Recalibration](/wiki/The_Occupation_Recalibration "The Occupation Recalibration")" (S7E13) to take up acting full time. Penny is the original female lead in the show before being joined by [Bernadette Rostenkowski](/wiki/Bernadette_Rostenkowski-Wolowitz "Bernadette Rostenkowski-Wolowitz") and [Amy Farrah Fowler](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler") in seasons 3 and 4, and in season 8, started working at the same company as Bernadette.

Since the pilot, she has always been Leonard's love interest, with the two dating briefly in the first episode of the second season, for most of the third season, and they rekindled their romance in "The Recombination Hypothesis". As of "[The Gorilla Dissolution](/wiki/The_Gorilla_Dissolution "The Gorilla Dissolution")", she and Leonard became engaged and were married at the start of season 9 in The Matrimonial Momentum.

Even though she is considered part of the guys' group, she represents the "dumb blonde" for viewer context in the series with many street smarts and communication skills to compensate for her lack of academic knowledge.

## Physical Appearance\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny is a slender, young woman with fair skin, blond hair and wears different types of clothing, mainly tank tops and jeans.

When she first moved into apartment 4B, she wore a light blue t-shirt, jean short shorts and brown boots.

## Personality\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny is somewhat naive and not thoroughly educated but has a lot of common sense and street smarts. Her dream is to become a famous actress, a goal she never seems to waver from until season 8. She is very kind-hearted and empathetic toward people though she can blow up when made mad, which prompted Leonard to refer to her as The Incredible Hulk" after she went off on Howard. She believes most guys are nice and has been hurt a lot. When someone shocks her, she tends to bat her eyes at them while considering her response. She also walks away when frustrated with people like Sheldon or situations she can't believe or understand. She knows how to throw out wise-cracks and is very loyal to her man as long as she is not betrayed. She also tends to deny doing embarrassing things, or she suddenly realizes they are embarrassing. In the first season, she seemed very naive but has appeared smarter in later seasons and more complicated in situations with her female friends. She also has a habit of being selfish and throwing her friends under the bus. For example, she sold Sheldon out to the court officials for running a red light, despite the fact he had done it to help her after she had dislocated her shoulder, simply because she didn't want the ticket.

### Season 1\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

[![Penny blackmails Sheldon](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/warner-bros-entertainment/images/2/21/Bbt-sheldon-penny.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/180?cb=20220512040537)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/warner-bros-entertainment/images/2/21/Bbt-sheldon-penny.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20220512040537)

[](/wiki/File:Bbt-sheldon-penny.jpg)

Penny blackmails Sheldon

In the [first episode](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot") Penny moves into Apartment 4B across from Apartment 4A where Leonard and Sheldon live. She had broken up with her boyfriend Kurt because he cheated on her. She asked the guys for a favor to go get her TV from his apartment, but he steals their pants and Penny apologizes for everything and later the three go out to dinner with Howard and Raj.

In "[The Big Bran Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Big_Bran_Hypothesis "The Big Bran Hypothesis")", Penny asks Leonard and Sheldon to sign for her delivery of her entertainment center. When Sheldon and Leonard, they discover that Penny's apartment is a mess, prompting Sheldon to try to clean it. When Penny arrives, they leave. Unbeknown to her at night, Sheldon cleans up the apartment anyway. When Penny wakes up the next morning, she is infuriated that Sheldon and Leonard came into her apartment while she was asleep, and forces Leonard to give back her spare keys. Sheldon forcefully apologizes to Penny and reveals that he cleaned her apartment. Penny bumps into Raj and she explains the situation, although Raj can't speak to her, he is a good listener, Penny decides to forgive Leonard, and when Leonard tries to apologize, she immediately forgives him.

### Season 2\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

[![Sheldon helping Penny get an enchanted sword](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/warner-bros-entertainment/images/4/4e/2x03-The-Barbarian-Sublimation-penny-and-sheldon-22774835-1580-888.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/180?cb=20220512040725)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/warner-bros-entertainment/images/4/4e/2x03-The-Barbarian-Sublimation-penny-and-sheldon-22774835-1580-888.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20220512040725)

[](/wiki/File:2x03-The-Barbarian-Sublimation-penny-and-sheldon-22774835-1580-888.jpg)

Sheldon helping Penny get an enchanted sword

After a post-date disagreement, Penny remains friends with all four guys, becomes an integral part of the Social Group and very good friends with Leonard.

In "[The Hofstadter Isotope](/wiki/The_Hofstadter_Isotope "The Hofstadter Isotope")", Penny is asked out on a date by Stuart and things end later in the next episode after it is revealed she called Stuart "Leonard".

In the season finale "[The Monopolar Expedition](/wiki/The_Monopolar_Expedition "The Monopolar Expedition")", Penny wishes Leonard wasn't going to the North Pole and even gives Leonard a blanket as a good luck gift on his expedition to the North Pole.

### Season 3\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

When the guys return from the North Pole, Penny has missed Leonard enough to express her feelings for him, and they date for most of the season.

Penny introduces her friend Bernadette to Howard as part of a Girlfriend Pact made between Howard and Leonard. Things don't go too smoothly until the two of them find out they both have overbearing mothers.

### Season 4\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D7&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny resumes being part of the guys group and has her own friends, Bernadette, along with Sheldon’s new girlfriend, [Amy](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler"). Also she realizes that she still has feelings for Leonard, especially since Leonard is dating Priya.

### Season 5\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D8&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Half way through the season (on the 100th episode), Leonard asks Penny out and they reunite, though Penny has misgivings.

### Season 6\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D9&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny works through her doubts and has a stronger relationship with Leonard, as she is now able to say "I love you" to him. They discuss marriage.

### Season 7\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D10&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny finds out she is legally married to Zack after Leonard, Sheldon and Amy tell her that weddings in Las Vegas wedding chapels are real when the two thought they were fake. At the end, she and Zack fill out annulment papers and the marriage is legally annulled ("[The Thanksgiving Decoupling](/wiki/The_Thanksgiving_Decoupling "The Thanksgiving Decoupling")"). Penny quits The Cheesecake Factory to concentrate on acting ("[The Occupation Recalibration](/wiki/The_Occupation_Recalibration "The Occupation Recalibration")") and becomes engaged to Leonard after she gets over her clash with the director who fired her ("[The Gorilla Dissolution](/wiki/The_Gorilla_Dissolution "The Gorilla Dissolution")").

### Season 8\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D11&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Between the finale of Season 7 and the premiere of Season 8, Penny drastically changes her look by swapping her usual long blonde locks for a short blonde pixie crop, a look she sports throughout the entire season. She gets a new job at Bernadette's company as a pharmaceutical rep, making excellent progress in her field and spending the year as Leonard's fiancée. At the end of the season, she suggests they head to Vegas to get married.

### Season 9\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D12&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Leonard's little make-out session at sea makes their marriage have a rocky start, but they quickly reconcile though they don't move out of Sheldon's apartment (because of Sheldon going through a bad breakup and due to Sheldon's abandonment issues). At the end of the season, when it's revealed that everyone is upset about not being part of the wedding due to their elopement, Penny suggests having a redo wedding ceremony.

### Season 10\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D13&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

In "The Conjugal Conjecture" Penny and Leonard have their re-wedding ceremony in a park which is officiated by Bernadette.

Penny and Leonard finally have their own apartment, Apartment 4A. In "[The Cohabitation Experimentation](/wiki/The_Cohabitation_Experimentation "The Cohabitation Experimentation")", Amy's apartment suffered water damage, was uninhabitable and she needed a place to stay. Sheldon and Amy started a five week experiment to see if they could manage living together and moved into Penny's old apartment, Apartment 4B. It turned into a permanent arrangement in "[The Veracity Elasticity](/wiki/The_Veracity_Elasticity "The Veracity Elasticity")". Penny also redecorates her and Leonard's bedroom.

### Season 11\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D14&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

While Sheldon proposes to Amy, he gets a call from Leonard and Penny, asking about where he is. He tells them about his unwilling kiss with Ramona and how it made him realize his true feelings about Amy. At the same time, Bernadette tells Penny that she’s pregnant again.

### Season 12\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D15&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Sheldon and Amy win the Nobel prize with Penny, Leonard, Howard, Bernadette and Raj coming to watch his speech. He then tells the story of his family who has changed his life. Penny And Leonard are soon to be parents.

Post claims Penny from Big Bang Theory "was a prostitute... implied in the show" and befriended the guys because they were furthest from clients. Pilot canon has her describing her screenplay about a girl from Lincoln, Nebraska who comes to LA to be an actress and ends up a waitress at the cheesecake factory, clarifying "No, I'm from Omaha!" https://the-big-bang-theory.com/quotes/character/Penny/ (pilot quote). No episode, writer or producer source lists sex work as her job; promiscuity is a running slut-shaming joke, but analysis notes she had roughly five confirmed partners vs Raj's at least 10 https://screenrant.com/big-bang-theory-penny-raj-sleep-together/ , undermining conflation of dating jokes with prostitution. The only "prostitute" lines are jokes: e.g. Penny in "The Financial Permeability" asks "That I'm some sort of Chinese food prostitute?" https://the-big-bang-theory.com/quotes/quote/941/ , and season 2 episode "The Vegas Renormalization" features a separate prostitute character Mikayla, not Penny. Darker original unaired pilot female lead Katie (Amanda Walsh) was described as darker/street-hardened and taking advantage of Sheldon/Leonard, but she was scrapped and replaced by Penny https://www.thethings.com/the-big-bang-theory-chuck-lorre-leonard-sheldon-roommate-katie-penny-kaley-cuoco/  — not canon evidence Penny was a prostitute.

## Penny Hofstadter

  
**Penelope "Penny" Hofstadter** is the show _The Big Bang Theory_'s first and always main female protagonist. She lives in [Apartment 4B](/wiki/Apartment_4B "Apartment 4B") with her husband Leonard Hofstadter across the hall from Sheldon Cooper, who lives in apartment 4A where Leonard used to live with Sheldon as roommates. Although the sleeping arrangements are a little complicated. This was an accommodation for Sheldon who was having a very hard time dealing with his break-up with Amy, and Leonard moving out in The 2003 Approximation. Leonard also maintains an office in 4A. Her full first name is possibly "Penelope" as implied by "[The Barbarian Sublimation](/wiki/The_Barbarian_Sublimation "The Barbarian Sublimation")", and her maiden name has never been revealed. But due to her recent marriage to Leonard, her last name is Hofstadter. For a while her last name was Johnson while unknowingly married to ex-boyfriend Zack Johnson. That marriage was annulled in [The Thanksgiving Decoupling](/wiki/The_Thanksgiving_Decoupling "The Thanksgiving Decoupling").

An aspiring, but mostly unsuccessful actress, she was born on a farm near Omaha, Nebraska, and worked at The Cheesecake Factory as a waitress until she quit in "[The Occupation Recalibration](/wiki/The_Occupation_Recalibration "The Occupation Recalibration")" (S7E13) to take up acting full time. Penny is the original female lead in the show before being joined by [Bernadette Rostenkowski](/wiki/Bernadette_Rostenkowski-Wolowitz "Bernadette Rostenkowski-Wolowitz") and [Amy Farrah Fowler](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler") in seasons 3 and 4, and in season 8, started working at the same company as Bernadette.

Since the pilot, she has always been Leonard's love interest, with the two dating briefly in the first episode of the second season, for most of the third season, and they rekindled their romance in "The Recombination Hypothesis". As of "[The Gorilla Dissolution](/wiki/The_Gorilla_Dissolution "The Gorilla Dissolution")", she and Leonard became engaged and were married at the start of season 9 in The Matrimonial Momentum.

Even though she is considered part of the guys' group, she represents the "dumb blonde" for viewer context in the series with many street smarts and communication skills to compensate for her lack of academic knowledge.

## Physical Appearance\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny is a slender, young woman with fair skin, blond hair and wears different types of clothing, mainly tank tops and jeans.

When she first moved into apartment 4B, she wore a light blue t-shirt, jean short shorts and brown boots.

## Personality\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fwarnerbros.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny_Hofstadter%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny is somewhat naive and not thoroughly educated but has a lot of common sense and street smarts. Her dream is to become a famous actress, a goal she never seems to waver from until season 8. She is very kind-hearted and empathetic toward people though she can blow up when made mad, which prompted Leonard to refer to her as The Incredible Hulk" after she went off on Howard. She believes most guys are nice and has been hurt a lot. When someone shocks her, she tends to bat her eyes at them while considering her response. She also walks away when frustrated with people like Sheldon or situations she can't believe or understand. She knows how to throw out wise-cracks and is very loyal to her man as long as she is not betrayed. She also tends to deny doing embarrassing things, or she suddenly realizes they are embarrassing. In the first season, she seemed very naive but has appeared smarter in later seasons and more complicated in situations with her female friends. She also has a habit of being selfish and throwing her friends under the bus. For example, she sold Sheldon out to the court officials for running a red light, despite the fact he had done it to help her after she had dislocated her shoulder, simply because she didn't want the ticket.
